column3: Near-exact Pharaoh parallel: threatened rule answers Musa with killing sons and sparing women.
Defines corruption as harming the land while withholding repair, clarifying the focus verdict.
Adds the irony that corrupters may not recognize their own corruption.
Directly restates Pharaoh's slaughter of sons and preservation of women as severe oppression.
Immediate sequel gives the divine reversal: the weakened are to become leaders and heirs.
Connects corruption to blocking others from God's way and multiplied consequence.
A second direct recollection of Pharaoh's same gendered persecution, now framed as deliverance.
Musa's journey toward Midian does not clarify Pharaoh's partitioning or persecution.
Only supplies a general designation of those who turn away as corrupters.
Directly characterizes Pharaoh as exalted and excessive, illuminating his self-elevation.
Its life-and-death distinction offers only a remote counterpoint to the focus oppression.
God's true exaltedness provides a distant contrast to Pharaoh's wrongful elevation.
Recounts Pharaoh's renewed order to kill believers' sons and spare their women.
Immediate continuation completes the reversal by promising settlement and exposing Pharaoh's fear.
The parable of powerless false gods does not add to the focus social mechanism.
Shows the formerly weakened inheriting the land while Pharaoh's constructed order is destroyed.
Within the same surah, gives Pharaoh and his forces' final overthrow in the sea.
Spreading indecency is a different form of social corruption, with only a broad channel resonance.
Shows Pharaoh policing belief by coercively treating independent assent as political conspiracy.
Divine choosing of servants does not clarify the focus oppression.
Distinguishes arrogant self-exaltation from rightful high status, sharpening the meaning of Pharaoh's elevation.
Places Musa's mission to Pharaoh among the recurring fate of corrupters.
Musa's marriage and work agreement does not develop the focus mechanism.
Condemns religious fragmentation into factions, closely echoing the focus division into shi'a.
Shows the later social reality of factional conflict inside Pharaoh's city.
Supplies a secondary instance of elites calling a messenger weak and relying on group power.
A contrast reading about false descriptions of God adds no focused support.
Recognition likened to knowing sons has no material link beyond the shared offspring term.
The infant Musa's nursing arrangement does not clarify the focus ayah.
Layered punishment for leading others astray only broadly parallels responsibility for systemic harm.
Restates division into exultant factions, adding the self-satisfied result of fragmentation.
The Pharaoh context is retained, but gratitude and punishment do not add to the persecution account.
Pharaoh labels Musa a corrupter while threatening murder, exposing the ruler's coercive inversion.
Names Pharaoh among corrupters at his final failed confession.
A same-surah vertical reversal of the self-exalted Qarun supplies a parallel outcome.
The highest horizon is unrelated to political elevation or corruption here.
Links unjust killing and corruption, making the focus slaughter a social-scale violation.
Signs and divine awareness do not add to the focus mechanism.
A command to glorify the Most High is too general to illuminate Pharaoh's conduct.
A group undertaking a distinct communal task only distantly parallels division into a faction.
Same-surah antithesis explicitly rejects seeking elevation and corruption in the land.
Describes rulers multiplying corruption, a broad structural parallel to Pharaoh's regime.
Recognition compared with knowing sons adds no relevant relation.
Shows the need for a remnant that restrains corruption before societies are ruined.
Portrays corruption as breaking covenants and social bonds, extending the focus judgment.
A faction's attempt to mislead supplies only a limited parallel to targeted domination.
Same-surah Pharaoh's exclusive sovereignty claim and tower project enact his self-exaltation.
Directly joins great self-exaltation with twice causing corruption in the land.
Links arrogant denial with wrongdoing and the fate of corrupters.
The consequences of spreading a report offer only a remote social-corruption parallel.
Warns that failed protective solidarity produces widespread disorder and corruption.
Depicts persistent pursuit of corruption and war, but not the focus's selective oppression.
Another concise account of Pharaoh and his army being seized and cast into the sea.
Its exhortation concerning conflict and being uppermost does not clarify the focus.
Directly names oppressed men, women, and children under a town's unjust rulers.
Threatened slaughter in Solomon's bird narrative is not the focus political practice.
Adds the false claim of being reformers when prohibited from corrupting the land.
Party affiliation is present, but it concerns faithful allegiance rather than oppressive partition.
Worship and concealed knowledge do not develop the focus ayah.
Pits arrogant elites against believers counted among the weakened, closely mirroring the social hierarchy.
Its tactical division into groups is procedural and unrelated to Pharaoh's fragmentation.
The greater punishment has no focused connection to the focus ayah.
Explains corruption as the result of competing ultimate authorities, a conceptual contrast to Pharaoh's monopoly claim.
Shows a faction's planned manipulation of belief, adding a secondary mechanism of division.
The elevated garden is unrelated to wrongful worldly elevation.
The elevated register of the righteous does not clarify the focus contrast.
Cosmic ordering of the earth provides no focused addition.
Defines corruption as destroying cultivation and progeny, closely extending the focus attack on communal continuity.
Same-surah instruction rejects seeking corruption in the land, directly countering Pharaoh's conduct.
Recognizes weakness in a military ratio, not imposed social weakening.
General trial of a town does not illuminate Pharaoh's regime.
A denial of causing corruption in a theft dispute gives only a lexical contrast.
Contrasts divided groups with divine aid that makes believers prevail over their enemies.
God's transcendence over partners does not add to the focus mechanism.
Mary's withdrawal from her family is unrelated.
Distinguishes reform from corruption in care for vulnerable orphans, a secondary ethical counterpoint.
The cow description and slaughter do not clarify Pharaoh's policy.
Weak descendants facing loss offer only a distant vulnerability parallel.
Abraham's ransom sacrifice is unrelated to the focus's coerced killing.
God's highest likeness is not a focused parallel to Pharaoh's elevation.
The term shi'a denotes affiliation here, but without the focus's imposed fragmentation.
Lot's plea for help against a corrupt people supplies a general response to systemic corruption.
The earth made habitable and its paths do not illuminate the focus ayah.
God's supreme sustaining authority only broadly contrasts with Pharaoh's claimed dominance.
Explicitly depicts people made into factions and turned against one another as a form of punishment.
Promises that apparent position and forces will prove weaker, a reversal of worldly dominance.
Doubled punishment for a distinct offense does not clarify the focus.
Describes kings corrupting towns and humiliating their honored people, a close political parallel.
Marital affection and mercy do not add to the focus's social order.
The root echo in doubled reward does not materially clarify imposed weakening.
Past peoples led from the path offer only a broad corruption outcome.
Internal division behind apparent collective strength is a distant factional parallel.
Transgression by prior communities is only a general wrongdoing parallel.
Inventing religious prohibitions and misleading people provides a remote injustice parallel.
Others rejoicing at harm does not clarify the focus mechanism.
The divine attributes of hearing and knowing add no focused relation.
The believers' delight in a garden is unrelated.
Calling revelation human speech does not add to the focus ayah.
Denial and turning away supply only a generic opposition parallel.
Demanding the promised punishment is unrelated to Pharaoh's partition and persecution.
Musa recalls Israel's rescue from Pharaoh as a defining divine favor, supplying the liberation frame.
The oppressed community voices harm before and after Musa's arrival, exposing the lived duration of Pharaoh's rule.
Near-exact repetition of Pharaoh's severe torment: killing sons and sparing women.
Names fear of Pharaoh and his chiefs, calls him exalted in the land, and shows belief constrained by persecution.
Musa identifies Pharaoh and his chiefs' wealth and splendor as instruments of leading people astray.
God's commission to Musa begins by naming Pharaoh's transgression.
The joint commission to Musa and Harun again identifies Pharaoh as having transgressed.
The warning of punishment for denial and turning away provides a remote consequence frame for Pharaoh.
The command to take God's servants out by night supplies the escape side of the oppressive situation.
Explicitly describes Pharaoh and his chiefs as arrogant.
Musa's commission to go to Pharaoh initiates the confrontation with the oppressive ruler.
Names Pharaoh's people as a people of wrongdoing in the commission narrative.
Musa calls Pharaoh's claimed favor the result of having enslaved the Children of Israel.
The night departure of the servants follows the Pharaoh confrontation and evokes their release from his control.
Introduces the Musa-Pharaoh account as a truthful narrative for believers, framing the focus scene.
The command protecting Musa as an infant supplies the maternal response to Pharaoh's threat against sons.
Pharaoh's wife explicitly forbids killing the infant, a pointed counteraction to the regime's infanticide.
Same-surah account of Pharaoh and his forces arrogantly exalting themselves in the land.
Completes Pharaoh's role by calling him and his followers leaders who summon to the Fire.
Groups Pharaoh with Haman and Qarun in arrogant rejection and failed escape from God.
Links Musa's mission to Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun, locating the oppression in a ruling network.
Pharaoh's command to build a tower enacts his self-authorizing political spectacle.
His tower project culminates in dismissing Musa's God, displaying arrogant denial.
Pharaoh publicly claims ownership of Egypt and its rivers, making his territorial domination explicit.
Pharaoh manipulates and diminishes his people until they obey him, closely explaining his rule over them.
Describes the testing of Pharaoh's people through an honorable messenger.
The messenger demands that Pharaoh's people release God's servants, directly opposing their subjection.
Recalls the rescue of the Children of Israel from humiliating torment.
Musa's sign sent to Pharaoh provides a concise later reference to the confrontation.
Pharaoh turns away with his forces and brands the messenger a sorcerer or madman.
Records that Pharaoh's people received warnings, a broad narrative precursor to their downfall.
Pharaoh's wife seeks rescue from Pharaoh and his deeds, giving an internal witness to his wrongdoing.
Places Pharaoh among the peoples who committed the overreaching offense.
Uses Pharaoh's received messenger as a warning precedent for the present audience.
States that Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger and was seized with a ruinous seizure.
Musa is sent to Pharaoh because he has transgressed.
Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord is the starkest verbal enactment of his self-exaltation.
Reports God's exemplary punishment of Pharaoh, completing the elevation-to-downfall pattern.
Names Pharaoh of the stakes among the destructive tyrannical powers of the past.
